sections.name: Password-Gate Intro

fields.text: This summer I worked as the sole UX design intern on SailPoint's identity security team, designing for enterprise administrators who manage access across thousands of applications.
fields.label: Intro paragraph 1

fields.text: The full account walks through the three-iteration redesign, the customer research that reshaped it, and the trust patterns now heading into beta. Inside:
fields.label: Intro paragraph 2

fields.text: The final design is validated with 10 enterprise customers, now in beta with a target of routing 10% of new source configurations through the wizard.
fields.label: Intro paragraph 3

sections.name: Password-Gate Image
Key Takeaway 1

fields.text: 🎯 Autonomy, calibrated to risk.
fields.label: Label

fields.text: A failed conversational prototype led me to a principle I now apply to any AI feature: match how much the AI decides to the cost of being wrong. It shaped every decision in the product that followed.
fields.label: Text

fields.text: 🔍 Transparency is not clarity.

fields.text: My first inline design showed all of the AI's reasoning at once. In A/B testing, users didn't know where to click or what their actions would lead to. The fix was letting admins choose when to see it.

sections.name: [para] Identity administrators are responsible for every access decision Sail…

fields.text: Identity administrators are responsible for every access decision SailPoint helps automate. I redesigned its AI-assisted source configuration experience across three iterations, moving from scripted chat to contextual recommendations with reasoning on demand, recovery when AI fails, and explicit approval when the consequences get higher. The redesign cut setup time by 60% and expanded into editing and provisioning as a reusable human-in-the-loop interaction model.

fields.text: The first version walked admins through a scripted chat with fixed prompts and fixed next steps. It narrated controls already visible on screen, duplicated actions elsewhere in the form, and turned simple configuration decisions into a linear conversation that could not actually respond. It had the cost of conversation without the benefit of one.

fields.text: I moved recommendations out of the dedicated chat panel and into the fields they actually affected. AI could now explain system state instead of narrating the interface, but my first inline version overcorrected on transparency. A single field could show an info icon, confidence score, AI-generated label, and success state at once. I had made the AI more visible, but harder to interpret.

fields.text: Customer feedback showed that admins wanted to verify recommendations, inspect their sources, and ask deeper questions when something felt wrong. I reduced the competing signals to one wand that appears when the admin wants more, opening a drawer with Overview for the recommendation, Deep Dive for reasoning and sources, and Ask Harbor Pilot for anything the structured workflow cannot answer.

The transition was designed to feel progressive rather than heavy handed, moving from a quick recommendation, to supporting rationale and sources, to open-ended help only when needed. fields.text: Error handling and recovery

sections.name: [para] This prototype shows what happens when the AI gets something wrong. In…

fields.text: This prototype shows what happens when the AI gets something wrong. Instead of blaming the admin for a failed recommendation, the flow clearly attributes the failure to the system and offers a way forward: suggested fix, retry, manual edit, or Harbor Pilot. The impact was not just better messaging, but a more trustworthy experience, because failure became something admins could recover from instead of a dead end.

fields.text: Loading state redesign

sections.name: [para] This prototype captures a smaller but important trust moment: waiting.…

fields.text: This prototype captures a smaller but important trust moment: waiting. The original loading state was just a pulsing dot and a generic label, which gave no sense of what the AI was doing during longer generation times. I redesigned it to show visible progress across each step, making the transition from "working" to "done" feel more transparent and reducing the sense that the system was stalled or uncertain.

sections.name: [image] From a pulsing dot to visible progress: each step shown as it complete…

fields.text: From a pulsing dot to visible progress: each step shown as it completes, so admins can tell working from stuck.

sections.name: [para] This prototype shows how the interaction model extends into provisioni…

fields.text: This prototype shows how the interaction model extends into provisioning, where the stakes are higher because recommendations can affect real access. The flow separates AI recommendation from admin approval, so the transition from suggestion to action is always explicit. That distinction helped carry the broader principle of the project forward: AI can speed up the work, but the admin stays responsible for the final decision.

fields.text: Provisioning: AI recommends a rule, the admin reviews it, and nothing takes effect until it's explicitly approved.

sections.name: [carousel] carousel

fields.text: Personas
Personas

Two personas built to bracket the range we actually saw in research, not just two individuals. Together they covered the bulk of who showed up to the machine: someone optimizing for speed, someone optimizing for connection, which meant the redesign had to hold both instead of picking one.
Storyboards
Storyboards

Storyboards walked each persona through the existing flow start to finish, panel by panel. Both stories ended the same way regardless of who was walking through them, standing at the machine, seeds in hand, no idea what they'd gotten, which is what made identification the priority over anything else.
Crazy 8s
Crazy 8s

Eight rapid concepts each, physical and digital, forced volume before judgment before a single final screen existed. One sketch cut the envelope dispenser outright instead of trying to clarify it, and that's the idea that survived into the shipped redesign.
Ideation
Ideation

Every research finding got turned into a How Might We before anyone reached for a solution. Identification and community kept surfacing as the two problems no concept was allowed to skip, which is why they became the redesign's actual spine.

fields.text: Count hidden until you expand
Questions were available, but the number of open items was hidden. Analysts could access the detail, but triage still required opening individual rows.
V1: questions nested under each part and collapsed by default, so triage means opening every row.
Grouping clustered questions, but urgency stays hidden until you expand every row
Flattened, but grouping lost
I surfaced more information directly in the table. This improved visibility, but weakened the grouping and made it harder to understand which questions belonged to which part.
V2: every question on its own row and fully visible, but structure and grouping are lost.
Status landed mid-row and interrupted the left-to-right scan
Count at a glance, detail on demand

I separated two different jobs: how many questions are open, shown immediately, and what those questions are, revealed on demand. Each row now shows a live question count for zero-click triage. Expanding the row reveals full detail while preserving the relationship between the part and its questions. I also added multi-select so analysts could act across multiple parts without opening each one individually.
V3: part grouping restored, with each question its own selectable row so triage can cross parts.
Reorder by part number
Per-question select, triage individual questions across parts

sections.name: [lede] UM GPT is the University of Michigan's AI platform for student group w…

fields.text: UM GPT is the University of Michigan's AI platform for student group work, free, private, and already in wide use. This started as an SI 307 assignment. After earning top marks, I kept going, using Claude, Lovable, and Figma Make as active design partners rather than just faster tools. What I found surprised me: none of the three features I built got a usable first draft. Every one needed a correction that only became visible once I checked the output against what students had actually told me. That correction, not the features themselves, is the real subject of this case study.

sections.name: [section] Why I used AI, and where it kept stopping short

sections.name: [para] This started as an SI 307 assignment. After it shipped, I kept going, …

fields.text: This started as an SI 307 assignment. After it shipped, I kept going, deliberately using Claude, Lovable, and Figma Make as design partners to see how far they'd take real product work.

sections.name: [para] The answer was consistent: far enough to be useful, not far enough to …

fields.text: The answer was consistent: far enough to be useful, not far enough to be done.

sections.name: [para] The tools were genuinely strong at two things. Speed, a working protot…

fields.text: The tools were genuinely strong at two things. Speed, a working prototype in minutes instead of hours. And structure, layouts that held together on the first pass. That let me explore more directions than a manual process would.

sections.name: [para] Every feature hit the same ceiling, and the Summarize Chat shortcut is…

fields.text: Every feature hit the same ceiling, and the Summarize Chat shortcut is where I first saw it clearly. A shortcut should hand you a summary in one step. Instead, the AI built a four-screen guided workflow. Every screen worked, but that was the problem: it optimized for thorough when the whole job of a shortcut is fast. A user who wants depth can just keep chatting. The AI couldn't tell those two intentions apart, so it defaulted to the more elaborate one every time.

sections.name: [para] That was the pattern under all three challenges: functional, structura…

fields.text: That was the pattern under all three challenges: functional, structurally fine, and wrong about what the user actually needed. Overcoming it came down to three kinds of judgment, information hierarchy, interaction flow, and keeping people in context.

fields.text: Four tools, three copy-pastes, one student bouncing between all of them. Brainstorm in ChatGPT, migrate to Docs, lose formatting, ask Slack for feedback, lose the thread, finalize in Notion. Every workflow I watched repeated the same shuffle.

sections.name: [para] ChatGPT Teams had the shared workspace and no task management. Notion …

fields.text: ChatGPT Teams had the shared workspace and no task management. Notion AI had strong docs and kept AI solo. Google Docs plus Gemini assisted the writing and hid the prompts. Slack coordinated everything and integrated nothing. Each solved a piece. None connected them. That is an architecture problem, not a feature problem.

sections.name: [para] I used Claude to score ten feature ideas on pain severity, feasibility…

fields.text: I used Claude to score ten feature ideas on pain severity, feasibility and impact, not to decide for me but to force the trade-offs into the open. Three rose: task assignment, activity log, AI shortcuts. I deferred @-mentions and file attachments to v2 and committed to building three things deeply instead of ten shallowly.

The tool would generate something structurally sound and confident-looking. I'd hold it against the actual evidence from my interviews. In every case, something didn't match: sometimes a missing field, sometimes a wrong default, sometimes an entire wrong shape of screen. Closing that gap was my job, not the tool's.

sections.name: [section] Making task assignment feel effortless

fields.text: Challenge 1
Making task assignment feel effortless

sections.name: [para] If creating a task felt like extra work, students would just text each…

fields.text: If creating a task felt like extra work, students would just text each other. The fix had to live inside the conversation.

sections.name: [para] AI could produce a create-task form instantly; that was never the prob…

fields.text: AI could produce a create-task form instantly; that was never the problem. What it couldn't do was make assigning feel like part of the conversation instead of a detour out of it. Its drafts treated task creation as a destination, a full form in its own space, a context switch. So I asked myself where the friction actually lived, and it wasn't in the fields, it was in the leaving.

sections.name: [para] I rebuilt it around interaction flow. Highlighting AI output surfaces …

fields.text: I rebuilt it around interaction flow. Highlighting AI output surfaces a contextual action inline; a side panel slides in with defaults pre-filled and the conversation still visible. In testing I watched this land: participants assigned their first task in 48 seconds on average, against the two-plus minutes the same action takes in Trello or Asana. One participant looked at the task card and said, "Oh, this is like Trello but... better? The AI context is huge." That was the moment I knew the in-context bet had paid off, they recognized the pattern instantly, but the conversation-awareness made it feel like more.

sections.name: [para] The delta: destination → in-context. AI could build the form. Making i…

fields.text: The delta: destination → in-context. AI could build the form. Making it disappear into the conversation was the design judgment.

sections.name: [section] Visibility Without Surveillance

fields.text: Challenge 2
Visibility Without Surveillance

sections.name: [para] Students wanted transparency without feeling watched. Instructors need…

fields.text: Students wanted transparency without feeling watched. Instructors needed to assess contribution. AI could build a metrics panel easily, and that was the trap: its instructor views defaulted to raw comparison, counts ranked side by side. When I put that concept in front of interview participants, three of seven recoiled before I'd even shown them a finished screen, using words like judged and compared. Claude named the mechanism, social comparison theory, but naming it didn't fix it. So I asked myself what those three were actually reacting to, and it wasn't the data, it was being ranked against a peer.

sections.name: [para] The fix was a relabeling, not a rebuild. Raw counts became qualitative…

fields.text: The fix was a relabeling, not a rebuild. Raw counts became qualitative signals, "context-rich," "collaborator," language instead of numbers. That was a judgment about human dynamics, the kind of call a generation tool has no basis to make, because "more visible" and "more comfortable" pull in opposite directions and only a person weighing real reactions holds the line between them.

sections.name: [para] The delta: numbers → language. Same information need, opposite emotion…

fields.text: The delta: numbers → language. Same information need, opposite emotional result.

sections.name: [section] Shortcuts Without Paralysis

fields.text: Challenge 3
Shortcuts Without Paralysis

sections.name: [para] Students kept retyping the same prompts, and my first instinct was to …

fields.text: Students kept retyping the same prompts, and my first instinct was to give them everything: a shortcuts menu with twelve options. When observing the usability test participants, that instinct fell apart, students froze for eight-plus seconds just scanning the list. Decision paralysis. One asked the question that became my standard: "why do I have to leave the conversation?"

sections.name: [para] This is where AI's instinct and mine had made the same mistake in diff…

fields.text: This is where AI's instinct and mine had made the same mistake in different directions, I over-offered, AI over-built. The Summarize shortcut from Section 01 was the pattern: asked for lightweight actions, AI kept generating elaborate multi-step flows, each internally sensible, none of them actually a shortcut. So I asked myself what a shortcut fundamentally is, and the answer was subtraction, not addition. I narrowed to four fixed actions, always visible below the input, and imposed one rule the tools couldn't infer: no new screen, answer inline, identical pattern across all four.

sections.name: [para] I kept four for reasons the testing bore out: they covered roughly 80%…

fields.text: I kept four for reasons the testing bore out: they covered roughly 80% of the AI interactions I'd observed, a fixed position let users build muscle memory, and icons plus labels stayed scannable in under two seconds. Five of five participants found and used the shortcuts without any instruction.

sections.name: [para] The delta: guided workflow → single action. AI optimized for thorough;…

fields.text: The delta: guided workflow → single action. AI optimized for thorough; a shortcut's whole job is efficient.

sections.name: [section] The distance between functional and intuitive

fields.text: Takeaway
The distance between functional and intuitive

sections.name: [para] AI moved fast and stayed structurally sound, and it stopped at the sam…

fields.text: AI moved fast and stayed structurally sound, and it stopped at the same place every time, functional but not intuitive. It could generate a task form, a metrics panel, a summary flow; it couldn't tell that the form needed to disappear into the conversation, that the panel needed to protect a student's dignity, or that a shortcut's whole value is doing less, not more. Those are judgments about interaction flow, keeping people in context, and information hierarchy, the last mile from working to usable, and every time, they came from watching a real person, not from a better prompt. AI is a genuine accelerator; it got me to a functional draft in a fraction of the time. But the distance between functional and intuitive is exactly the distance a designer is for, and closing it, three times, deliberately, was the actual work.
